q: What does shutil.copy do when the destination is an existing folder?
options: It replaces the whole folder with the one file
It raises FileExistsError because the folder exists
It puts a copy inside that folder under the source file's name
It copies the file's content into a file named like the folder
why: A folder destination keeps the file's name; a file name destination becomes the copy's name.

q: What must be true of the destination of shutil.copytree when no option is given?
options: It must already exist as an empty folder
It must be on the same drive as the source
It must have the same name as the source
why: copytree raises FileExistsError if the destination exists.

q: How does shutil.copy2 differ from shutil.copy?
options: It also tries to keep metadata such as the modification time
It copies two files at once
It writes the contents twice for safety
It refuses to overwrite an existing file
why: copy2 keeps metadata where it can; copytree uses it for every file.

q: What does dirs_exist_ok=True change in shutil.copytree?
options: It deletes the existing folder first and then copies
It continues into an existing folder, overwriting same-named files and leaving the others
It skips every file whose name already exists there
It copies, then raises an error at the end
why: Files of the same name are overwritten; other files in the destination stay.

q: Where does shutil.move put a file when the destination is an existing folder?
options: Next to the folder, under the folder's name
Inside that folder, under its own name
why: Moving into a folder keeps the name; across file systems it is a copy followed by a delete.

q: When does shutil.move act as a rename?
options: Only when the destination is on another drive
Only when the new name is longer than the old
When the destination is not an existing folder, so it is taken as the new path
why: A destination that is not a folder is the new path, so a move inside one folder renames.

q: A folder already holds a file with the name of the file you shutil.move into it. What happens?
options: shutil.Error is raised and nothing is moved
The old file is silently overwritten, as the chapter says
The new file gets a number added to its name
The old file is sent to the recycle bin
why: This is a place where Python 3.14.4 differs from the chapter's statement.

q: From which Python version can a Path object copy and move itself?
why: Path.copy, copy_into, move and move_into arrived in 3.14.

q: What is the difference between os.unlink and os.remove?

why: Both delete one file for good.

q: Which folders can os.rmdir delete?
why: A folder that still holds something raises OSError.

q: Which statement about shutil.rmtree is correct?

It moves the folder to the trash
It deletes the files but keeps the folders
why: There is no recycle bin and no question; the deletion cannot be undone.

q: Which rmtree parameter replaces the deprecated onerror and receives the exception itself?
why: onexc exists since Python 3.12.

q: What is a dry run?
options: Running a program with all output switched off
Running a program twice to compare the results
Running a program with the dangerous call replaced by a print, to see what it would do
Running a program on a copy of the disk
why: A dry run shows the effect first, which finds a typo such as *.rxt before anything is deleted.

q: What does the third-party send2trash module do?
options: Deletes a file securely by overwriting it
Frees the disk space at once
Empties the trash from a program
Moves a file or folder to the trash so it can be restored
why: It is not part of the standard library and frees no space.

q: What does os.listdir return?
options: A list of the names of the entries in one folder
A list of the paths of all files below the folder
A list of Path objects for the files only
A sorted list of the subfolders
why: It looks at one folder only and promises no order.

q: What does Path.iterdir yield?
options: Only the files of the folder
A Path for each entry of one folder, without looking into subfolders
Every file in all the subfolders
why: Like listdir it stays in one folder and promises no order.

q: How does Path.rglob differ from Path.glob?

why: rglob is glob applied to the folder and all folders below it.

q: Which three values does os.walk give on each pass?

The parent folder, the file path and the extension
The file name, its folder and its depth
The current folder, its subfolder names and its file names
why: Names come without paths.

q: Which os.walk argument gives subfolders before the folder that holds them?
why: That is the order needed to delete a tree with rmdir.

q: How can a top-down os.walk loop skip a subfolder?

By removing its name from the subfolder list in place
why: os.walk looks at the same list object again; a new list is ignored.

q: Why is renaming files during an os.walk loop, as the chapter does, acceptable?
options: os.walk copies the whole tree first
The documentation guarantees that every rename is listed
It only renames files and never adds or removes folders
why: The documentation leaves it open whether a renamed file is listed.

q: Since which Python version does Path.walk exist?
why: Path.walk was added in Python 3.12.

q: What does opening a ZipFile in mode 'w' do to an existing ZIP file of that name?
options: It empties it and starts a new archive
It opens it for reading only
why: Mode 'a' adds; mode 'x' refuses.

q: Which compression method does ZipFile use when none is given?
why: The chapter recommends ZIP_DEFLATED.

q: What does a higher compresslevel for ZIP_DEFLATED mean?
options: An archive protected by a password
More effort: slower and usually smaller
why: Levels run from 0 to 9.

q: Which ZipFile mode adds to an existing archive and keeps what is there?
why: 'w' erases first, 'x' refuses an existing file, 'r' reads.

q: What does ZipFile.namelist return?
options: The names of the archive's members, as a list of strings
The names of the files that were not compressed
A dictionary of names and sizes
The names of the files on disk that were added
why: Folders appear with a closing slash.

q: Which ZipInfo attribute holds the size of a member inside the archive?
why: file_size is the original size.

q: Which kind of data compresses least?
options: The same text repeated many times
A file of only zero bytes
why: Repetition packs well; compressed data has little left to remove.

q: What does extractall do with a file of the same name in the target folder?
options: It adds a number to the new name
why: Check the target folder first.

q: What does extract raise for a member name that is not in the archive?
why: The name must be one that namelist returns.

q: What does the zipfile module do with a member name that contains .. when it extracts?
options: It extracts the file where the name points
It removes the dangerous part so the file stays in the target folder
It extracts it and marks it read-only
why: Even so, the documentation says not to extract untrusted archives without inspecting them.

q: How do the zip files of shutil.make_archive differ from ZipFile.write with no compression argument?
why: One call builds the archive from a whole folder.

q: How does shutil.unpack_archive choose the format?
options: From a format argument that is required
From the size of the file
From the extension of the archive's file name
why: An unknown extension raises ReadError.

q: How does the chapter's backup program choose a new archive name?
options: It counts up from 1 until a name does not exist yet
why: Each run makes the next numbered snapshot.

q: What happens to a folder that holds no files in the walk-and-write backup?
options: It is stored as an empty folder
It is not recorded in the archive
It is stored with a number added
why: Only files are written.

q: What does ZipFile.write store when given an absolute path and no arcname?
options: The path relative to the current folder
The whole path, less the drive letter and leading slash
The path with each folder replaced by a number
why: The arcname argument keeps the archive tidy.

q: Why can the chapter's snapshot be slightly larger than its files?
options: ZIP files can never be compressed
The archive was opened without a compression argument, so ZIP_STORED applies
why: Pass compression=zipfile.ZIP_DEFLATED to compress.

q: What goes wrong if the archive is created inside the folder being backed up?
options: The walk lists the new archive and the program writes it into itself
why: Put the archive elsewhere or skip it.

q: Which function copies a folder together with all its contents?
why: shutil.copy is for one file.

q: Why test the lower-cased file name when copying all the PDFs?
options: Because pathlib cannot read upper case
So the copy is stored in lower case
So that report.PDF is found as well as report.pdf
Because extensions are always lower case on Windows
why: The destination must also lie outside the tree being walked.

q: Which function gives a file's size in bytes for the large-files program?
why: The chapter's limit is 100MB.

q: What does str.zfill(3) do to the string '7'?
options: It pads it with zeros to '007'
It converts it to the integer 7
why: The width is the width of the numbers in the file names.

q: How does the date program turn 12-31-2020 into 31-12-2020?
options: It swaps the first two groups of a regular expression with sub
It reads the file's modification time
why: A name without a date is left alone.

q: Which module does the chapter use for copying, moving and renaming files and folders?
why: shutil is the first subject of the chapter.

q: Which two functions does the chapter use to copy?
options: shutil.copy for a folder and shutil.move for a file
shutil.copy for a file and shutil.copytree for a folder
why: copy is for one file; copytree takes the folder with everything in it.

q: How does the chapter treat moving and renaming?
options: As one operation, done with shutil.move
As two operations in separate modules
As renaming only, with moving done by os.walk
As a copy followed by a delete the program must write
why: A move whose destination is not a folder is a rename.

q: What are the chapter's two protections against a bug that deletes the wrong files?
options: A backup ZIP and a password
A dry run and the recycle bin
A longer file name and a log file
Running as administrator and a second copy of the program
why: Deleting is where the chapter warns most.

q: Which three calls delete for good?
why: None of them uses the recycle bin.

q: Which practice makes deletion safer?
options: Deleting only from a folder inside the current folder
Printing what would be deleted before deleting, or sending files to the recycle bin
why: Both protections let a person catch a mistake before it is permanent.

q: What are the two ways the chapter reaches the files of a folder?
options: Listing one folder and walking a whole tree of folders
why: Listing stays in one folder; walking enters every subfolder.

q: What do os.listdir and Path.iterdir have in common?
options: Both list one folder and do not enter its subfolders
why: Neither promises an order.

q: Which tool does the chapter use to do something to every file in a folder and all folders below it?
why: os.walk gives three values on each pass.

q: Which module creates, reads and extracts ZIP archives?
why: The chapter's third section is about zipfile.

q: What does writing an archive start with?
options: Opening a ZipFile in a mode and writing files into it
why: Mode 'w' creates, 'a' adds and 'x' refuses an existing file.

q: What does reading an archive start with?
options: A ZipFile object opened on its file name
A call to os.listdir on the archive
why: namelist and getinfo are then asked of that object.

q: Which two ZipFile methods take files out of an archive?
why: extractall takes everything; extract takes one member.

q: How do shutil.make_archive and shutil.unpack_archive relate to the chapter?
options: They are the chapter's main tools
They are in the Python documentation but not in the chapter
why: They are a one-call alternative to the zipfile loops.

q: What does Project 5 of the chapter do?
options: Backs a folder up into numbered ZIP files
Copies a folder to a second drive every night
Deletes the oldest files of a folder
why: Each run makes the next numbered snapshot.

q: What does the backup program work out first?
options: The list of files to delete
why: The name is the folder's last part, an underscore and a number.

q: After choosing a name, what does the backup program do?
options: Walks the folder and writes every file into the archive
why: One loop inside another covers the whole tree.

q: What does chapter 11 end with?
options: Six practice questions and one project
A summary, four practice questions and four practice programs
why: The practice work follows the backup project.

q: What do the practice questions test?
why: They ask what the functions are and how they differ.

q: Which topics do the four practice programs apply?
options: Walking, copying, sizes, numbering and regular expressions
why: They are applications of the chapter's own tools.
